## Setup R

::: fragment
```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
# install.packages("rsdmx")
library(quarto)       # for compiling Quarto presentations and documents
library(rsdmx)        # for fetching SDMX data
library(tidyverse)    # dplyr, ggplot2, readr, etc.
library(here)         # path settings
library(plotly)       # for interactive plots
library(countrycode)  # for country codes
library(lubridate)    # for date handling
```
:::

## What is SDMX?

-   **S**tatistical **D**ata and **M**etadata e**X**change
    -   International standard for exchanging statistical data and metadata
    -   Initiated by 7 international organizations:
        -   BIS, ECB, Eurostat, IMF, OECD, UN, World Bank
    -   Used by 100+ national and international organizations

::: fragment
-   Why SDMX matters:
    -   Standardized data structures across providers
    -   Machine-readable metadata (concepts, codelists)
    -   Direct access to official statistics at the source
:::

## Interfaces to Official Statistics

-   Packages or set of classes and methods to read data through exchange frameworks
    -   Use [R](https://www.r-project.org/) (or [Python](https://www.python.org/)) packages to read data from APIs
        -   Individual packages:
            -   [eurostat](https://cran.r-project.org/package=eurostat): Access data from Eurostat
            -   [OECD](https://cran.r-project.org/package=OECD): Access data from the OECD API
    -   General-purpose packages:
        -   [rsdmx](https://cran.r-project.org/package=rsdmx): Direct access to SDMX endpoints (Eurostat, ECB, OECD, IMF, etc.)
        -   [pxweb](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/pxweb/vignettes/pxweb.html): R package for PX-Web API (Statistics Sweden, Estonia)

## Exploring SDMX Providers

::: fragment
```{r}
# List available built-in providers
providers <- getSDMXServiceProviders()
provider_df <- as.data.frame(providers)
provider_df[, c("agencyId", "name")] |> head(10)
```
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Key Providers for Economic Statistics

| Provider | Agency ID | Data Coverage |
|----------|-----------|---------------|
| Eurostat | ESTAT | EU official statistics |
| ECB | ECB | Monetary & financial data |
| OECD | OECD | Economic indicators |
| IMF | IMF_DATA | Balance of payments, etc. |

## Example: Fetch Unemployment Data

-   Example data: Unemployment rate, ILO definition, total, Estonia, from Eurostat
-   Using `readSDMX()` function with the ESTAT provider

::: fragment
```{r}
#| cache: true
# Fetch unemployment data from Eurostat
unemp_sdmx <- readSDMX(
  providerId = "ESTAT",
  resource = "data",
  flowRef = "ei_lmhr_m",
  key = "M.PC_ACT.SA.LM-UN-T-TOT.EE",
  start = 2000,
  end = 2025
)

# Convert to data.frame
unemp <- as.data.frame(unemp_sdmx)
```
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

```{r}
glimpse(unemp)
```

## Understanding SDMX Keys

-   The **key** specifies which data to fetch
-   Format: `dimension1.dimension2.dimension3...`
-   For Eurostat ei_lmhr_m dataset:

| Position | Dimension | Value | Meaning |
|----------|-----------|-------|---------|
| 1 | FREQ | M | Monthly |
| 2 | UNIT | PC_ACT | % of active population |
| 3 | S_ADJ | SA | Seasonally adjusted |
| 4 | INDIC | LM-UN-T-TOT | Total unemployment |
| 5 | GEO | EE | Estonia |

## Work with the dataframe

We need to standardize column names (SDMX uses different conventions)

```{r}
# Standardize the data
unemp <- unemp |>
  mutate(
    period = ym(obsTime),  # Convert to date
    value = as.numeric(obsValue),
    provider_code = "Eurostat",
    dataset_code = "ei_lmhr_m",
    series_code = "M.PC_ACT.SA.LM-UN-T-TOT.EE"
  )

# Extract metadata
(source_name <- unique(unemp$dataset_code))
(provider_code <- unique(unemp$provider_code))
(country_name <- "Estonia")
(series_id <- unique(unemp$series_code))
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: slide
# Plot the data
p1 <- ggplot(unemp, aes(x = period, y = value)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = paste("Unemployment Rate in", country_name),
    subtitle = paste("Monthly, seasonally adjusted —", provider_code),
    x = "Date", y = "Percent",
    caption = paste("Source:", provider_code, "| Dataset:", source_name, "| ID:", series_id)
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
p1
```

## Interactive plot

When working with dynamic documents, I can also create interactive plots using the `plotly` package.

```{r}
ggplotly(p1)
```

## But I Need a Plot That Matches Eesti Pank's Corporate Design

-   Use **ChatGPT** to extract the official color palette and font settings from Eesti Pank's design templates (e.g., *Tööturu_ülevaade_2025.xlsx*)
-   Define a **custom `ggplot2` theme** that matches the corporate look - `theme_ep()`

::: fragment
```{r}
library(ggplot2)

# Color scale
scale_color_ep <- function(...) {
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "#0079BC", # Accent 1
      "#D6E1F2", # Accent 2
      "#FF8C42", # Accent 3
      "#8ACC61", # Accent 4
      "#E85C70", # Accent 5
      "#E091D4" # Accent 6
    ),
    ...
  )
}

# Fill scale
scale_fill_ep <- function(...) {
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "#0079BC",
      "#D6E1F2",
      "#FF8C42",
      "#8ACC61",
      "#E85C70",
      "#E091D4"
    ),
    ...
  )
}
# Custom ggplot2 theme for Eesti Pank
theme_ep <- function(base_size = 11, base_family = "") {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size, base_family = base_family) %+replace%
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#FFFFFF", color = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#FFFFFF", color = NA),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "#858A8C"),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      axis.text = element_text(color = "#000000"),
      axis.title = element_text(color = "#000000"),
      plot.title = element_text(
        face = "bold",
        color = "#000000",
        margin = margin(b = 10)
      ),
      plot.caption = element_text(size = 9, color = "#444444", hjust = 0),
      legend.background = element_rect(fill = "#FFFFFF", color = NA),
      legend.key = element_rect(fill = "#FFFFFF", color = NA),
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.title = element_blank(),
      legend.margin = margin(b = 5),
      legend.box.margin = margin(t = 5, b = 5)
    )
}

```
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: slide
unemp |>
  filter(period >= "2010-01-01") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = period, y = value)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "#000", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "1 year",
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_number(suffix = "%"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  labs(
    title = paste("Unemployment Rate in", country_name),
    subtitle = paste("Monthly, seasonally adjusted"),
    x = NULL,
    caption = paste(
      "Source:",
      provider_code,
      "| Dataset:",
      source_name,
      "| ID:",
      series_id
    )
  ) +
  theme_ep()
```

## But I Need to Store the data as an Excel File

```{r}
library(openxlsx)

wb <- createWorkbook()
addWorksheet(wb, "Unemployment Data")
writeData(wb, "Unemployment Data", unemp)
saveWorkbook(wb, "teaching_materials/unemp_data.xlsx", overwrite = TRUE)
```

-   Exporting editable figures: Advanced topic!
    -   Use {officer} + {rvg} to embed editable vector graphics in Excel or use {mschart} to create editable charts for Powerpoint or Word

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### How do we find the series ID/key?

-   Go to the provider's data portal (e.g., [Eurostat Data Browser](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/))
    -   Search for the dataset you want
    -   Select filters/dimensions
    -   Look for "SDMX" download option or API query builder
-   Or use the rsdmx package to explore available datasets

## Fetching from ECB

-   Example: ECB Interest Rates (MIR - MFI Interest Rate Statistics)
-   Estonia mortgage rates: loans to households for house purchase

::: fragment
```{r}
#| cache: true
# ECB uses direct URL approach
ecb_url <- "https://data-api.ecb.europa.eu/service/data/MIR/M.EE.B.A2C.A.R.A.2250.EUR.N?startPeriod=2010&endPeriod=2025"

mir_sdmx <- readSDMX(ecb_url)
mir <- as.data.frame(mir_sdmx)

# Standardize
mir <- mir |>
  mutate(
    period = ym(obsTime),
    value = as.numeric(obsValue)
  )

head(mir[, c("period", "value", "TITLE")], 3)
```
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: slide
mir |>
  ggplot(aes(x = period, y = value)) +
  geom_line(color = "#0079BC", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Estonia Mortgage Interest Rates",
    subtitle = "Loans to households for house purchase (new business)",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Interest Rate (%)",
    caption = "Source: ECB MIR Statistics"
  ) +
  theme_ep()
```

## Fetching from OECD

-   OECD updated their API in July 2024 (OECD Data Explorer)
-   Requires direct URL approach with new format

::: fragment
```{r}
#| cache: true
# OECD Consumer Confidence Index - Composite Leading Indicators
oecd_url <- "https://sdmx.oecd.org/public/rest/data/OECD.SDD.STES,DSD_STES@DF_CLI/.M.LI...AA...H?startPeriod=2015-01&endPeriod=2025-12"

cci_sdmx <- readSDMX(oecd_url)
cci <- as.data.frame(cci_sdmx)

# Preview
head(cci[, c("REF_AREA", "obsTime", "obsValue")], 5)
```
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

```{r}
#| warning: false
# Filter for European countries and standardize
cci_eu <- cci |>
  filter(REF_AREA %in% c("EU27_2020", "AUT", "EST", "FIN", "DEU", "LVA", "LTU", "POL", "SWE")) |>
  mutate(
    period = ym(obsTime),
    value = as.numeric(obsValue),
    country = case_when(
      REF_AREA == "EU27_2020" ~ "EU27",
      TRUE ~ countrycode(REF_AREA, origin = "iso3c", destination = "country.name")
    )
  )

unique(cci_eu$country)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
library(gghighlight)

desired_order <- c("European Union", "Austria", "Germany", "Estonia",
                   "Finland", "Lithuania", "Latvia", "Poland", "Sweden")

p3 <- cci_eu |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = "solid", size = 0.25) +
  geom_point(
    data = cci_eu |> group_by(country) |> slice_max(period),
    aes(x = period, y = value, color = country),
    shape = 16
  ) +
  geom_line(aes(x = period, y = value, color = country)) +
  gghighlight(
    use_direct_label = FALSE,
    unhighlighted_params = list(colour = alpha("grey85", 1))
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = cci_eu |> group_by(country) |> slice_max(period),
    aes(x = period, y = value, color = country, label = round(value, 1)),
    hjust = -0.5,
    vjust = 0.5,
    size = 2.5,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    date_labels = "%Y",
    date_breaks = "2 years",
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = c(96, 98, 100, 102, 104),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ factor(country, levels = desired_order)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Composite Leading Indicator",
    subtitle = "Selected European Countries & EU27",
    caption = "Source: OECD / rsdmx"
  )
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

```{r}
#| echo: false
p3
```

## Summary: rsdmx Patterns

| Pattern | Code Example |
|---------|--------------|
| Built-in provider | `readSDMX(providerId = "ESTAT", resource = "data", flowRef = "dataset", key = "...")` |
| Direct URL | `readSDMX("https://data-api.ecb.europa.eu/service/data/...")` |
| Wildcarding | Use empty position in key: `"M..SA.."` or `NULL` in list |
| Get labels | Use `dsd = TRUE` parameter, then `as.data.frame(sdmx, labels = TRUE)` |

## Key Takeaways

1.  **SDMX** is the international standard for statistical data exchange
2.  **rsdmx** provides direct access to official statistics at the source
3.  Different providers may require different approaches (built-in vs URL)
4.  Always standardize column names (`obsTime` → `period`, `obsValue` → `value`)
5.  Use provider data portals to discover dataset codes and key structures
